title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Comprehensive Guide (Customer Requirements, Day‑2 Ops, Upgrade/Rollback)
author: Ethan Chen
content:
Overview

This document is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference private deployments (VPC-hosted private control plane and on‑prem packaged deployments). It consolidates: reference architectures, customer requirements, packaging and install notes, day‑2 operations runbooks, and safe upgrade/rollback procedures. It is intended for SREs, platform engineers, solutions engineers, and customer infrastructure teams.

Scope and audience
- Scope: VPC private deployments (customer VPC with Redwood control plane connectivity when required) and on‑prem air‑gapped package installs. Covers pre‑reqs, network/security, sizing, packaging, installs, day‑2 ops, upgrades, and rollbacks.
- Audience: eng-private-deployments, customer infra teams, Redwood solutions engineers, and support oncall.

High level reference architectures
1) VPC deployment (recommended for cloud customers)
- Components: customer VPC, private subnet for runtime nodes, NAT/egress, optional private link to Redwood control plane, KMS integration for keys, customer-managed logging sink (S3/AZBlob/GCP) and metrics export (Prometheus remote_write).
- Flow: User requests -> Internal app -> Redwood runtime in customer VPC (model serving) -> Optional control plane calls (over PrivateLink/VPN) for telemetry and billing.
- Deployment footprint: 3+ availability zones, autoscaling group per availability zone, dedicated GPU subpools per model family for isolation.

2) On‑prem deployment (air‑gapped / regulated environments)
- Components: air‑gapped runtime cluster (k8s or systemd/docker-compose), local artifact registry, HSM/KMS integration (optional), offline evaluation harness, local observability (Prometheus/Grafana).
- Flow: Admin triggers local inference runtime with prepackaged model artifacts; control plane optional via customer sync adapters.

Customer requirements library (summary)
Below is a condensed table of common customer requirements we track. For each customer engagement the solutions team creates a tailored copy of this table with non‑functional thresholds filled.

Requirement ID | Category | Required | Description | Owner
REQ-001 | Network | Mandatory | Private connectivity method: Direct Connect / VPN / PrivateLink required for control plane communication unless air‑gapped. | Solutions Eng
REQ-002 | Security | Mandatory | KMS/HSM integration for encryption-at-rest; customer-managed keys required for regulated customers. | Security
REQ-003 | Compliance | Optional/Mandatory | Data residency and retention policy; specify regions and retention windows. | Customer/Legal
REQ-004 | Capacity | Mandatory | Target sustained throughput (tokens/sec) and 95th percentile latency SLO per endpoint. | Product/Customer
REQ-005 | Monitoring | Mandatory | Prometheus metrics exposed, alerting hooks for SLO breaches and disk/GPU errors. | Eng-SRE
REQ-006 | Backup | Mandatory | Configuration & model artifact backup frequency; database backups retention. | Eng-Platform

Pre‑deployment checklist (network, security, infra)
- Network: CIDR ranges, subnets for runtime and control plane, NAT vs egress, firewall rules (20.20.0.0/16 example), PrivateLink endpoints or VPN termination IPs.
- Identity: Service account creation, least privilege IAM roles, RBAC bindings for Kubernetes installs.
- Keys & secrets: KMS/HSM key ARNs, secret rotation window, vault access policy.
- Storage: Object store endpoint, bucket names, lifecycle policy for model artifacts, minimum IOPS for model stores.
- Capacity: GPU SKU (e.g., NVIDIA A100, H100), node sizing (vCPU, RAM), expected pod density.
- Compliance: Audit logging destination, required retention window (e.g., 90/365 days), SIEM integration details.

Example preflight verification commands
- Network: curl --connect-timeout 5 https://redwood-control.example.internal/healthz (verify routing / PrivateLink)
- KMS: aws kms describe-key --key-id <key-id> --region <region>
- Storage: aws s3 ls s3://<bucket> --no-sign-request (verify access from runtime VPC)

On‑prem packaging & install notes
Supported packaging forms:
- Kubernetes Helm chart (recommended for k8s envs)
- OP‑PACKAGE tarball for systemd/docker-compose installs (for air‑gapped)
- Container images hosted in customer registry (pull policy: IfNotPresent for air‑gapped)

Supported OS and prerequisites:
- Linux distros: Ubuntu 20.04+, RHEL 8+, Rocky Linux 8+
- Docker: 20.x+, containerd supported for k8s installs
- Kernel: 5.4+ recommended for GPU driver compatibility
- GPU drivers: NVIDIA driver matching container-runtime and CUDA requirements (see packaging/driver-matrix.md)

Sample Helm values snippet (redacted):
```yaml
image:
  repository: registry.customer.local/redwood/runtime
  tag: 2026.02.18
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
    cpu: 8
    memory: 64Gi
nodeSelector:
  accelerator: nvidia-a100
persistence:
  modelStore:
    type: s3
    s3:
      endpoint: https://s3.customer.local
      bucket: redwood-models
```

Installation steps (k8s Helm)
1. Ensure CRDs installed: kubectl apply -f crds.yaml
2. Create namespace and secrets: kubectl create namespace redwood && kubectl create secret generic redwood-secrets --from-literal=KMS_KEY=<key>
3. Install Helm chart: helm install redwood-runtime ./charts/redwood -f my-values.yaml --namespace redwood
4. Verify pods: kubectl wait --for=condition=available deploy -l app=redwood-runtime --timeout=10m

Day‑2 operations (runbooks & SLOs)
Key SLOs and metrics to monitor:
- Latency SLOs: P95 <= configured latency (example: 150ms for small-context models)
- Availability SLO: 99.95% monthly uptime for dedicated model endpoints
- Error budget: 0.05% monthly error budget — triggers SRE review if burned more than 25% in a rolling 7‑day window

Essential dashboards and alerts:
- Runtime health: GPU memory utilization, NVLink errors, OOM kills
- Serving metrics: tokens/sec, requests/sec, P50/P95 latency, active-connections
- Storage: model store error rate, object fetch latency
- Infra: node CPU/Memory, disk usage > 70% alerts, kubelet restarts

Routine day‑2 procedures:
- Add capacity: 1) Update autoscaling policy, 2) Provision nodes in AZ, 3) Verify pod distribution and GPU allocation.
- Replace GPU node: cordon -> drain -> replace -> uncordon, verify model caches warm-up.
- Backup model store: run model-store-snapshot.sh and verify checksums.

Incident triage quick steps
1. Identify scope: single pod, AZ, or global. Check recent deploys and autoscaler events.
2. Mitigate: reroute traffic to healthy model variant or increase replica counts.
3. Recover: restart pods or rollback (see Upgrade & Rollback).
4. Postmortem: update incident tracker and link runbook changes.

Upgrade and rollback procedures (safe, canary-first pattern)
Principles: test in staging, automated canary rollout with traffic shifting, automatic validation gates (smoke tests, perf checks), and manual rollback step with validated artifact.

Canary upgrade summary (example)
1. Build and push new image, tag with semantic version (e.g., 2026.02.20-canary).
2. Deploy canary pool (10% of traffic) in a single AZ: helm upgrade --set canary.enabled=true --set canary.weight=10 -f canary-values.yaml
3. Run automated validation: unit smoke tests, end‑to‑end latency checks, quality checks against a small eval prompt set.
4. Monitor for 30–60 minutes for error rates, latency regressions, and resource anomalies.
5. If green, increase to 50% then 100% with pauses and validations between steps.

Rollback checklist (immediate rollback scenario)
- Preconditions: last known good image tag, DB schema compatibility matrix indicates no destructive migrations in the failed release.
- Steps: 1) Pause traffic to canary: modify traffic weights, 2) helm rollback release to previous revision: helm rollback <release> <rev>, 3) If DB migrated and incompatible, follow DB rollback runbook (restore snapshot and run migration-revert scripts), 4) Validate runtime health and run smoke tests, 5) Communicate incident and next steps to stakeholders.

Important safety notes
- Always assume a rollback window: keep the last good artifact available for at least 72 hours after upgrade.
- For migrations: prefer backward compatible, two‑phase migrations (deploy code that can read both schemas, then migrate, then remove fallback).

Ownership, support, and escalation
- Owners: eng-private-deployments (primary), eng-sre (oncall support), security (KMS/compliance questions), solutions-eng (customer onboarding).
- Oncall escalation path: 1) Platform oncall -> 2) Serving runtime owner -> 3) Engineering director. Use PagerDuty policy: REDWOOD-PD-PRIVATE.
- Runbook updates: any change to the procedures or thresholds must be committed to this page and reviewed by eng-sre.

Appendix: useful commands and references
- Check pod GPU allocation: kubectl get pods -o=custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,GPUs:.spec.containers[*].resources.limits
- Force rollback example: helm rollback redwood-runtime 3 --namespace redwood
- Model store snapshot example: ./scripts/model-store-snapshot.sh --bucket s3://redwood-backups --prefix customer-x --verify
